blocks.title: Libraries
bullets: Generally, libraries are bits of code written by you or others that you can use in your program.
Python allows you to share functions or features with others as "modules".
If you copy and paste code from an old project, chances are you can create such a module or library that you could bring into your new project.

blocks.title: Think of Libraries as A Swiss Army Knife

leftPanel.label: Real Life Analogy
leftPanel.title: A Swiss Army Knife
leftPanel.description: Instead of manufacturing a knife, scissors, and file from scratch, you import a tool with everything pre-built.

blocks.question: Why do we import libraries instead of writing all code ourselves?
blocks.answer: Libraries contain pre-written, tested code by other developers, saving us time and making our programs more reliable.

blocks.title: Command-Line Arguments
bullets: What if we wanted to be able to take input from the command-line? For example, rather than typing `python average.py`, what if we wanted to type `python average.py 100 90`?
`sys` is a module that allows us to take arguments at the command line. `argv` is within the `sys` module:

blocks.title: Command-Line Arguments Example
blocks.code:
import sys

print("hello, my name is", sys.argv[1])
blocks.expectedOutput: Run this code to see the result.

blocks.title: Command-Line Arguments
blocks.body: If you type `python name.py David`, you will see `hello, my name is David`. `sys.argv[1]` is where `David` is being stored. What is held in `sys.argv[0]`? If you guessed `name.py`, you would be correct!

blocks.title: Packages
bullets: One of the reasons Python is so popular is that there are numerous powerful third-party libraries. We call these third-party libraries, implemented as a folder, "packages".
PyPI is a repository or directory of all available third-party packages.
Python has a package manager called `pip` that allows you to install packages quickly. For example: `pip install cowsay`.

blocks.title: Packages Example
blocks.code:
import cowsay
import sys

if len(sys.argv) == 2:
    cowsay.cow("hello, " + sys.argv[1])
blocks.expectedOutput: Run this code to see the result.

blocks.title: Packages
bullets: You can find other third-party packages at [PyPI](https://pypi.org/).

blocks.title: APIs
bullets: APIs or "application program interfaces" allow you to connect to the code of others.
`requests` is a package that allows your program to behave as a web browser would. In your terminal, type `pip install requests`.
It turns out that Apple iTunes has its own API. The format returned is called JSON, a text-based format used to exchange data between applications.

blocks.title: APIs Example
blocks.code:
import requests
import sys

if len(sys.argv) != 2:
    sys.exit()

response = requests.get("https://itunes.apple.com/search?entity=song&limit=1&term=" + sys.argv[1])
print(response.json())
blocks.expectedOutput: Run this code to see the result.

blocks.title: APIs
bullets: Python has a built-in JSON library that can help us interpret the data received:

blocks.title: APIs Example
blocks.code:
import json
import requests
import sys

if len(sys.argv) != 2:
    sys.exit()

response = requests.get("https://itunes.apple.com/search?entity=song&limit=1&term=" + sys.argv[1])
print(json.dumps(response.json(), indent=2))
blocks.expectedOutput: Run this code to see the result.

blocks.title: APIs
bullets: How could we output just the track name?

blocks.title: APIs Example
blocks.code:
import json
import requests
import sys

if len(sys.argv) != 2:
    sys.exit()

response = requests.get("https://itunes.apple.com/search?entity=song&limit=50&term=" + sys.argv[1])

o = response.json()
for result in o["results"]:
    print(result["trackName"])
blocks.expectedOutput: Run this code to see the result.

blocks.title: APIs
bullets: You can learn more about `requests` through the [library's documentation](https://docs.python-requests.org/), and about JSON in Python's documentation of [JSON](https://docs.python.org/3/library/json.html).

Others are third-party packages that need to be installed using `pip`. You can make your own packages for use by yourself or others! In this lecture, you learned about…
